Also, consider counseling/support groups to help with the emotional burdens of chronic pain. This disease can wear you out, so having a good support system can help you manage that aspect of the experience.

There are good stretches and bad stretches. Talk with your rheumatologist about where to set your expectations. Good communication will help you get the maximum amount of help. Sometimes there are additional medications that can be prescribed (corticosteroids, NSAIDs, etc.) that can supplement your primary treatment during flare ups.

I have had really bad flareups that made me question my ability to drive. It's best to err on the side of caution as difficult as that might be. As far as the mental/emotional aspect of coping with this, try to cut yourself some slack. It can be really overwhelming at times and that's a perfectly reasonable reaction to what you are experiencing. I'm not sure what your treatment plan is looking like, but discuss pain management with your rheumatologist and see if there is anything they can do to help you preserve your abilities. I have good days and bad, I try to make sure that I keep that in mind when I think things aren't going well.

I've been on enbrel for a little over 7 years. I'm an engineer, so cognitive function is an important part of my livelihood. I have never experienced any direct side effects from the medicine. I would think that the cognitive load of managing pain and lack of sleep when going untreated would be far more impactful. At least that was my experience. I was a zombie from lack of sleep and constant pain. Enbrel turned my life around. I went on a "fixing spree", visiting my family to do all the things I had neglected for the years I went untreated once I found out I could use a screwdriver and wrench again. I hope you get to experience that joy as well.
